name: Collectr
tagline: Tracks a trading card and collectibles collection with market values, so you know what the shoebox is worth.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The app itself is a database with a nice skin: cards, quantities, conditions, purchase prices, current value, a chart that goes up or down. An agent can build that in a session, and for Magic and Pokemon you can even get real prices free from Scryfall and pokemontcg.io. What you cannot one-shot is the coverage: sealed product, sports cards, graded slabs, comics, one-off collectibles, all of that pricing is scraped and normalized from marketplaces and it is genuinely tedious work. Camera scanning of cards and a phone app you actually carry into a card shop are also out of reach for a weekend. So the DIY version is great if you collect one or two supported games and are happy typing on a laptop, and a downgrade otherwise.
coreLoopDIY: Search a card, add copies with condition and what you paid, then see current market value and cost basis for the whole collection with a value history chart.
requirements: Node 20 and a local machine to run it on
Free pokemontcg.io API key for Pokemon pricing (Scryfall needs none)
A cron job or manual click to snapshot prices daily
Willingness to type card names instead of pointing a camera at them
whatYouLose: Card scanning by camera, which is most of the actual convenience
A mobile app in your pocket at the shop or the show
Pricing coverage beyond whatever public APIs you wire up: no sealed, no graded comps, no sports cards
Automatic set and product data updates when new releases drop
Any social or portfolio-sharing layer, and someone else worrying about price feed breakage
moatNotes: The normalized cross-marketplace price history is the asset. The UI is the demo.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because collectors do not want to be data engineers. Paying gets you one place where a Charizard, a sealed booster box, a graded slab and a sports rookie card all have a defensible number next to them, updated without your involvement, on a phone you can hold up in a shop. A self-hosted tracker gives you the ledger, which is the easy half, and quietly leaves you maintaining scrapers for the hard half. If your collection is one game deep, that trade is fine. If it is broad, it is not.
notes: The ledger is a weekend; the price feed is a job.
prompt:
Build a local-first collection tracker for trading cards called Shoebox.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Next.js (App Router) with TypeScript and Tailwind
- SQLite via better-sqlite3, file at ./data/shoebox.db
- No auth, no accounts, no telemetry, no cloud. Single user on localhost.
- Secrets in .env.local, read via process.env. Provide .env.example.

Data sources:
- Magic: Scryfall API, no key needed. Respect rate limits with a simple delay.
- Pokemon: pokemontcg.io API, key from POKEMON_TCG_API_KEY in .env.local.
- Wrap each source behind a PriceProvider interface so more can be added later.

Features in scope:
1. Search page: type a card name, pick a game, show results with set, number, image thumbnail.
2. Add to collection: quantity, condition (NM, LP, MP, HP, DMG), foil boolean, purchase price, purchase date, optional note.
3. Collection page: sortable table of holdings with current market price per copy, line value, cost basis, gain or loss in currency and percent. Totals in a sticky footer.
4. A refresh action that re-fetches current prices for every distinct card in the collection and writes one row per card per day into a price_snapshots table. Idempotent per day.
5. Portfolio page: line chart of total collection value over time from price_snapshots, plus a flat cost basis line. Use a simple chart library, your pick, only one.
6. CSV import and export of holdings.

Explicitly out of scope, do not attempt:
- camera or image card recognition
- sealed product, graded slab comps, sports cards, comics
- any mobile app, native or PWA install flow
- user accounts, sharing, multiplayer

Seed the DB with 5 example holdings so the charts are not empty on first run. Include a scripts/snapshot.ts runnable with npm run snapshot for cron. README: setup in under ten lines, and a short honest section on which prices are real and which games are unsupported.
